Elias lived in a world of salt, iron, and rhythmic light. For-two years, he had been the keeper of the Blackwood Reach, a jagged tooth of rock that jutted out of the churning Atlantic. His life was measured not by calendars, but by the oil levels in the lamps, the polishing of the Fresnel lenses, and the steady, thrumming *thrum-thrum-thrum* of the rotating gears of the lighthouse’s great eye.

He was a man of few words, mostly because there was no one to speak to but the gulls, who were notoriously poor conversationalists. He liked the solitude; it was heavy, like a thick wool blanket, and protected him from the biting wind.

One Tuesday in October, following a gale that had shaken the very foundations of the tower, Elias went down for his morning patrol. The sea had been a beast for three days, sending waves crashing against the cliffs like physical blows. When the storm finally retreated, leaving the world dripping and gray, Elias descended the spiral staircase to the narrow wind-swept cove to check for debris.

The beach was a graveyard of kelp, shattered driftwood, and shattered glass. But there, nestled in a bed of emerald-green sea glass, was a flash of cobalt blue.

It was a bottle, thick and heavy, shaped by years of tumbling in sand. It was sealed with a cork held fast by a blackened wax. Elias picked it up, the glass surprisingly warm despite the cold air.

Back in the warmth of the kitchen, with a small fire crackling in the iron stove, Elias set the bottle on the scarred oak table. Using a small pocket knife, he pried away the wax. The cork popped with a sigh, releasing the scent of ancient air and salt. Inside was a scroll of parchment, tied with a piece of twine.

He unfurled it. He expected a map, or a desperate plea for help. Instead, he found a letter, written in a delicate, elegant script that had faded to a soft sepia tone.

*“To whoever finds this,”* it began. *“My name is Clara. I am writing this from a city that feels too small for my dreams, and a heart that feels longing for the smell of jasmine in the spring.”*

Elias read. For the next hour, the world outside the lighthouse blurred into the background. Clara wrote of a life in a crowded port, of the noise of the markets, and of the way she watched the horizon every evening, wondering what lay beyond the curve of the world. She wrote of a love that didn't return her, and a fear that she would spend her entire life in the only place she knew.

*“If you are reading this,”* the letter concluded, *“it means the sea has carried my hope where I could not. I hope you are somewhere the air is clear. I hope you have found the peace I am still desperately searching for.”*

Elias set the paper down. The ink was old—perhaps decades, perhaps a century. Clara
